newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Rights groups enraged by Israeli security adviser.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups enraged by Israeli security adviser.

text.p: Human rights groups on Tuesday blasted Israel's decision to appoint as a security adviser a former secret service agent who had allegedly killed Palestinian hijackers after taking them into custody.

An official in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office confirmed on Monday that Ehud Yatom, quoted last year as saying he used a rock to crush the skulls of two Gaza hijackers in 1984, was a member of a special council that advised the government on counter-terrorism.
The Palestinian Centre for Human Rights (PCHR) said in a statement from the Gaza Strip:
"The decision to appoint the criminal Yatom as an assistant to an adviser of the Israeli prime minister is the reward for a criminal who should be jailed."
"Yatom's appointment...reflects the extent of the ethical decline and moral level that the political system in Israel has reached," the statement said.

The Jerusalem-based Israeli Centre for Human Rights in the occupied territories said in a statement that Yatom was "a self-proclaimed killer" and urged the international community to prosecute him under the U.N. Convention against Torture.
"B'Tselem is shocked at the appointment of Ehud Yatom as special assistant to Meir Dagan, the prime minister's adviser on terrorism," B'Tselem said in a statement.
An official in Netanyahu's office said in response to a query on Monday that Yatom was "a member of a special council on counter-terrorism," but did not elaborate.
Israel's biggest newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, quoted Yatom last August as saying he killed two Palestinian hijackers who were captured after they seized an Israeli bus in 1984.

"We put them in our van and then I received instructions from (Shin Bet domestic security chief) Avraham Shalom to kill them, so I killed them with a big stone. I crushed their skulls," the newspaper quoted Yatom as saying.
The prime minister's office, under which the Shin Bet operates, denied at the time that Yatom made the comments. But the newspaper said it stood by its story.
After the killings, the Shin Bet mounted an elaborate coverup that led to the resignation of Shalom and three other top agency officials.
They received presidential pardons along with seven other agents, including Yatom.
